```{r data}
# Fifty countries, each variable averaged over 1960 to 1970.
life <- LifeCycleSavings

# Body weight (kg) and brain weight (g) for 62 species.
data(mammals, package = "MASS")


# The spread ratio: residual SD in the top third of fitted values --------------
# over the bottom third. Near 1 means the spread is even.
spread_ratio <- function(m) {
  third <- cut(fitted(m), quantile(fitted(m), 0:3 / 3), include.lowest = TRUE)
  s <- tapply(resid(m), third, sd)
  s[[3]] / s[[1]]
}

# Output -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# ≈ 1	Residual spread is similar across the range of predictions, consistent with constant variance
# > 1	Spread grows as predictions grow (the classic “fan” or “funnel” shape in a residuals-vs-fitted plot)
# < 1	Spread shrinks as predictions grow (a reversed funnel)


```

# Part 1 · Reading a model with four predictors (14 points)

### Model
Savings Rate is regressed onto % of population under 15; % of population over 75; disposable income per person; and growth rate

```{r}
full <- lm(sr ~ pop15 + pop75 + dpi + ddpi, data = LifeCycleSavings)
summary(full)
```

## (1a) The coefficient on pop15
```{r}
a1_coeff <- full$coefficients["pop15"]
a1_se <- summary(full)$coefficients["pop15", "Std. Error"]
a1_ci <- confint(full, "pop15")
a1_pval <- summary(full)$coefficients["pop15", "Pr(>|t|)"]
```
The coefficient for `pop15` is `r round(a1_coeff, 3)`. One percentage unit increase in `pop15` for a given country is associated with  a decrease of `r abs(round(a1_coeff, 3))` percentage points in saving rate, holding `pop75`, `dpi`, and `ddpi` constant. The SE for `pop15` is `r round(a1_se, 3)`, with a 95% CI of `r round(a1_ci, 3)`, and p-value of `r round(a1_pval, 3)`; indicating that the coefficient is significant.

## (1b) The coefficient on pop75
```{r}
b1_coeff <- full$coefficients["pop75"]
b1_se <- summary(full)$coefficients["pop75", "Std. Error"]
b1_ci <- confint(full, "pop75")
b1_pval <- summary(full)$coefficients["pop75", "Pr(>|t|)"]
```
The coefficient for `pop75` is `r round(b1_coeff, 3)` (CI: `r round(b1_ci, 3)`, p = `r round(b1_pval, 3)`) holding all other covariates constant. Any association between `pop75` and savings rate is not significant for this data. Since it has a large CI whose range is negative to positive, it cannot reliably tell us the direction of the association. At the very least, a positive association will not be large.

## (1c) What "holding constant" means here
Holding covariates constant means to hold the values for those covariates constant in the model while allowing a given predictor to vary to determine its association with the outcome and provide an estimate coefficient. It does not describe a comparison among countries, but that for a given country the estimate can be observed given the data.
"A percentage point increase in `pop15` results in a `r abs(round(a1_coeff, 3))` percentage point decrease in savings rate." A causal sentence like this is not supported by the data as the study design is observational only.
